headline: Episode 42: Is Lumen b a second Earth?
standfirst: The hosts chat about a newly found planet, its climate and its star
byline: Transcript of the Starlight Weekly podcast
brief: The hosts are enthusiastic, and a little careless. Find the claims that would not survive a physics check.

body.t: Welcome back, everyone. Today we look at Lumen b, a rocky planet orbiting a star about 40 light-years away.
Lumen b reflects 40% of the starlight that reaches it, an albedo of 0.40, so it absorbs only 40% of the incoming radiation.

options: A planet that reflects 40% absorbs 40% and emits the other 20%, because the three amounts must add up to 100%.
The reflected 40% is absorbed lower down in the atmosphere, so the planet absorbs all of the starlight.
Albedo is the fraction reflected, so the fraction absorbed is 1 − 0.40 = 0.60, or 60%.
feedback: Emission is a separate process: the planet radiates its own thermal energy. The starlight arriving is either reflected or absorbed, nothing else.
Radiation that is reflected goes back into space. It is not absorbed by the planet.
err.fix: Lumen b reflects 40% of the starlight that reaches it, an albedo of 0.40, so it absorbs the other 60% of the incoming radiation.
keys: Albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that is reflected.

body.t: Averaged over the whole planet, the intensity arriving is a quarter of the solar constant at that distance, because the planet's cross-section πr² is a quarter of its surface area 4πr².
body.ok: It is correct: the planet intercepts light over a disc of area πr², but that energy is shared over a sphere of area 4πr², so the average intensity is S/4.

body.t: At the temperature it has now, the planet radiates away exactly as much power as it absorbs, which is why its average temperature is steady.
body.ok: It is correct: a steady average temperature means absorbed power and emitted power are equal.

body.t: Its atmosphere is rich in carbon dioxide, and these greenhouse gases warm the surface because they absorb the incoming visible light from the star.

options: Greenhouse gases warm the surface by acting like a mirror, reflecting the star's visible light back down onto the ground before it can escape.
They absorb the infrared that the surface emits and re-radiate it in all directions, some of it back down.
They absorb the star's visible light and re-emit it as visible light in every direction, which is why the surface ends up warmer than expected.
feedback: Reflection of starlight would cool the planet by reducing the energy absorbed. The warming comes from absorbing infrared, not reflecting visible light.
Most of the star's visible light passes through a thin gas layer. The gases interact with the longer-wavelength infrared from the surface.
err.fix: Its atmosphere is rich in carbon dioxide, and these greenhouse gases warm the surface because they absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-radiate some of it back down.
keys: Visible light mostly passes through; the surface re-emits as infrared.
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-radiate it in all directions, returning some to the surface.

body.t: If the planet's greenhouse gases increase, less power escapes to space than the planet absorbs, and its average temperature falls until the two powers are equal again.

options: The temperature falls, because a thicker atmosphere always blocks more of the star's light.
The temperature stays the same, because the planet is already in equilibrium and more gas cannot change that.
Less power leaving than arriving is a net energy gain, so the temperature rises until the powers match.
feedback: A thicker greenhouse layer mainly affects the planet's emitted infrared. If emission drops below absorption, energy builds up and the planet warms.
More greenhouse gas upsets the old balance. The planet warms until a new equilibrium, at a higher temperature, is reached.
err.fix: If the planet's greenhouse gases increase, less power escapes to space than the planet absorbs, and its average temperature rises until the two powers are equal again.
keys: Absorbed power greater than emitted power means a net energy gain.
The temperature rises until a new, warmer equilibrium is reached.

body.t: To learn what the atmosphere holds, astronomers study the star's light after it has passed through the planet's atmosphere.
The dark lines they see appear because the atoms in the gas emit photons at those wavelengths, which makes the starlight at those wavelengths dimmer.

options: Atoms emit extra photons at those wavelengths, and the dark lines show where the emission is weakest.
Atoms absorb photons whose energy matches the gap between two energy levels, removing those wavelengths from the starlight.
The gas is transparent at those wavelengths, so the dark lines are wavelengths the star never produced.
feedback: Emission would add light at those wavelengths and give bright lines, not dark ones.
The star does emit those wavelengths. The atoms in the gas absorb them, because they have matching energy-level gaps. The lines identify the gas.
err.fix: The dark lines they see appear because the atoms in the gas absorb photons at those wavelengths, which removes light at those wavelengths from the starlight.
keys: Absorption lines are dark: atoms absorb photons matching energy-level gaps.
Photons of those wavelengths are missing from the transmitted light.

body.t: The wavelengths of those dark lines match the wavelengths of the bright lines the same gas would give when hot, because both come from the same gaps between energy levels.
body.ok: It is correct: absorption and emission by the same element involve the same energy-level differences, so the line wavelengths coincide.

body.t: Lumen itself is a main-sequence star, steadily fusing hydrogen in its core.
A second star has the same surface temperature as Lumen but twice its radius, so it radiates twice the power.

options: Luminosity goes as surface area, which goes as radius squared, so the star radiates four times the power.
Luminosity is proportional to the volume, which goes as the radius cubed, so the star radiates eight times the power.
Luminosity is proportional to the radius, so twice the radius gives twice the power.
feedback: A star radiates from its surface, not from its whole volume. The power radiated depends on surface area.
Power depends on surface area, not radius alone. Use $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ at the same temperature.
err.fix: A second star has the same surface temperature as Lumen but twice its radius, so it radiates four times the power.
keys: Doubling the radius gives four times the luminosity.
